meta.label: Home care services
meta.attribution: These scores describe home care brands and groups in England, not individual agencies. Many brands here are franchise networks, so one office's rating says little about the next, and the agency's own inspection report matters more than a brand's average. The inspection record is this catalogue's own count from the Care Quality Commission's published ratings file (as at 1 September 2026) joined to its care directory (23 September 2026). It covers agencies the directory lists as home care agencies that register no other service, because the ratings file no longer gives a location-level rating to agencies that also register supported living or other services. Locations are grouped by the name they trade under, or by the CQC brand name or provider name where the note says so. The score is the share rated Good or Outstanding among agencies rated Outstanding, Good, Requires improvement or Inadequate, rounded. Across the 6,221 rated agencies of this kind that share is 87.5 per cent, and 3,650 of the 9,894 have no published rating at all. It is not a CQC statistic and CQC does not endorse it. Ratings are snapshots: between 44 and 89 per cent of a brand's ratings were published more than three years before the file date, and each note gives its figure. Choice is the count of agencies divided by 1.8, capped at 95, and says nothing about capacity or fees. Fees are not scored, because each office of a franchise network sets its own prices and the pages found show prices from different areas. Transparency scores how much of a price a page read for this check shows: 90 for hourly, shorter-visit, weekend and overnight rates, 80 for a national starting hourly price with charges, 75 for branch pages that give some rates, 60 for weekly packages only, and 30 where a page says prices start from an affordable rate and gives no figure. It reflects the pages read, not every branch. Contains CQC data used under the Open Government Licence. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are regulated by other bodies and are not covered. This is not advice on choosing care. A council can carry out a needs assessment, and any agency should be asked for its latest inspection report before a decision. Reviewed 2026-09. Suggest changes via Contribute.

criteria.label: Inspection record: share of the brand's home care agencies in England rated Good or Outstanding by CQC
Choice: how many agencies it has, so how easily a family can find an office near them
How much of a price the brand's own pages show

products.name: Bluebird Care

safety.note: CQC's ratings file (as at 1 September 2026), joined to its care directory, lists 154 home care agencies that register no other service and are named Bluebird Care. 140 hold an overall rating: 27 Outstanding, 107 Good, 6 Requires improvement and 0 Inadequate, which is 95.7 per cent Good or Outstanding, against 87.5 per cent across the 6,221 rated agencies of this kind in England. 14 have no published rating. 69 per cent of the ratings were published more than three years before the file date, and 6 carry a rating inherited from an earlier provider.

accessibility.note: The CQC ratings file and care directory list 154 home care agencies that register no other service and are named Bluebird Care, 1.6 per cent of the 9,894 in England. Scored as agencies divided by 1.8, capped at 95; a bigger network is likelier to have an office near a given family, but this says nothing about capacity, waiting lists or fees.

transparency.note: Two branch pages were read. Bluebird Care's Calderdale page lists 30 minutes at £21.99, 45 minutes at £26.10 and 60 minutes at £28.99, and says the rates cover trained carers, consistent visits, care plans and supervision. A second branch page, linked, for Reading, Maidenhead and Windsor says home care visits 'start from £31.50' and live-in care 'from £1,650 per week', and gives no visit-length rates. Prices differ by branch, so this reflects the pages read.

products.name: Care arranged by your council after a needs assessment

transparency.note: The Department of Health and Social Care's charging circular for 2026 to 2027, published 17 February 2026, sets out the rules councils apply to people whose care is arranged by a local authority: the capital limits stay at £14,250 (lower) and £23,250 (upper), and it gives the minimum income guarantee for people receiving care other than in a care home, for example £241.45 a week for a single person of pension credit age. It is a national rulebook, so what a given person pays still depends on a council's financial assessment.

links.label: Apply for a needs assessment (GOV.UK, England and Wales)

focuses: Route that is not a private purchase
products.description: The route that is not a private purchase in England. A council assesses care needs, and people may then have care arranged for them and pay towards it depending on a financial assessment. GOV.UK's needs assessment page says services can include home care and lists a postcode lookup for the local council.
